title: Small Buildings and Architectural Design
description: How a small building is designed and drawn: site, programme, structure, light, heat and the drawings that describe it.
audience: Adults with school maths and physics who have not studied architecture.
outcomes: You'll be able to read a site and place a building by sun.
You'll be able to read plan, section and elevation and use scale.
You'll be able to compute a stair, a joist moment and a U-value.
You'll be able to judge light, condensation and comfort.

Approved Document L: Conservation of fuel and power (England)
Approved Document K: Protection from falling, collision and impact (stairs)

lessons.title: Reading a site: sun, wind and ground
lessons.objective: Compute noon sun heights and shadow lengths for a latitude and read what they mean for placing a building.

concepts.title: Noon sun altitude
concepts.summary: At noon the sun's altitude is 90 degrees minus latitude plus declination; the declination is +23.44 at June solstice and -23.44 at December solstice.

concepts.title: Orientation
concepts.summary: In the northern hemisphere the south face receives low winter sun and, with shading, little summer sun.

misconceptions: Learners think the sun rises due east and sets due west every day. That is true only at the equinoxes.
Learners think the south face is warmest because it faces the equator and so needs the most glass; unshaded, it overheats in summer.
Learners forget that the winter sun is the one that matters for heating.
sequence: A site is more than a plot: sun, wind, slope, access, neighbours, noise, views, water.
Why altitude changes through the year: the 23.44-degree tilt.
Formula and the three key dates.
Shadow length = height / tan(altitude).
Where to put long walls, glass and the garden.
Sketch a site analysis diagram.
examples: Latitude 52: June noon altitude 90-52+23.44=61.4; December 90-52-23.44=14.6.
A 6 m wall: shadow 3.3 m in June and 23.1 m in December.
A 0.6 m overhang above a south window casts a shadow 1.10 m deep in June and 0.16 m in December, which shades summer sun and admits winter sun.

figures.learnerAction: Slide the date and hour; see the ray angle and shadow length.

lessons.title: From brief to programme
lessons.objective: Turn a brief into a list of rooms, areas and adjacencies and compute gross area.

concepts.title: Programme
concepts.summary: The list of spaces a building must provide, with areas, relationships and requirements.

concepts.title: Net to gross
concepts.summary: Net area is room floor area; gross area adds walls, corridors and services, so gross = net / efficiency.

misconceptions: Learners start with the elevation instead of how people use the spaces.
Learners add room areas and treat the sum as the building footprint.
Learners ignore adjacency: kitchen next to dining, bathroom away from the front door.
sequence: Interview the client: who, how many, what happens daily.
List spaces and activities.
Give areas from furniture and circulation.
Draw a bubble diagram of adjacency.
Net-to-gross with efficiency about 85 percent for a small house.
Check against budget per square metre.
examples: Net 68 m^2 at 85 percent efficiency: gross 80 m^2.
At 2200 per m^2 the build cost is 176 000.
A 12 m^2 bedroom needs a double bed (1.4 x 2.0 m) plus circulation of 0.7 m on both long sides and the foot.

lessons.title: Plan, section and elevation
lessons.objective: Say what each of the three views shows and convert drawing lengths using scale.

concepts.title: Plan
concepts.summary: A horizontal cut about 1.2 m above the floor, looking down.

concepts.title: Section and elevation
concepts.summary: A section is a vertical cut seen from the side; an elevation is a view of an outside face without a cut.

concepts.title: Scale
concepts.summary: 1:50 means 1 unit on paper stands for 50 in the building.

misconceptions: Learners think a plan is a view from above; a roof plan is, but a floor plan is a cut.
Learners read a scale ratio the wrong way round.
Learners expect an elevation to show inside spaces.
sequence: Why drawings: communicate without the object.
Orthographic projection.
Plan cut and what is cut and what is seen below.
Section cut shows heights, floor build-up, roof.
Elevation shows face, openings, materials.
Scale and units.
examples: A room 4.2 m wide at 1:50 is 84 mm on paper; at 1:100, 42 mm.
A wall measured 120 mm on a 1:20 detail is 2400 mm in the building.
Floor-to-ceiling 2.4 m at 1:50 is 48 mm.

figures.shows: A small house cut away with a plan cut and a section cut shown as planes.
figures.learnerAction: Slide the cut plane up and down; the plan view changes.

figures.shows: A plan, section and elevation of the same room set side by side.
figures.learnerAction: Hover a window in one view to highlight it in the others.

lessons.title: Moving through a building
lessons.objective: Size a stair from storey height and check access widths and ramps.

concepts.title: Stair rule
concepts.summary: Riser R and going G satisfy 2R + G between 550 and 700 mm; about 630 mm is comfortable.

concepts.title: Circulation
concepts.summary: The space people use to get between rooms: halls, corridors, stairs.

misconceptions: Learners fix the stair length first and the rise falls out wrong.
Learners think steeper is only a comfort issue; it is a falling hazard.
Learners forget headroom.
sequence: Circulation is the movement space between rooms and is part of the brief.
A stair starts from the floor-to-floor height, not from the length.
Choose a riser near 175 mm and divide the height into a whole number of risers.
Use 2R + G = 630 mm for a comfortable going.
Total run = (number of risers - 1) x going.
Check width, headroom, doors and any ramp at no steeper than 1:12.
examples: Floor-to-floor 2700 mm: 16 risers of 168.75 mm; going 630-337.5=292.5 mm; 15 goings = 4387.5 mm run.
With 175 mm risers, 2R+G=630 gives G=280.
Ramp rise 0.6 m at 1:12 is 7.2 m long.

figures.shows: Stair section with rise, going, nosing and headroom marked.
figures.learnerAction: Change the riser and see the going and run.

figures.shows: Plan of a hallway with door swings and a 1525 mm turning circle.

lessons.title: Holding a small building up
lessons.objective: Trace a load path and size a timber floor joist.

concepts.title: Load path
concepts.summary: The continuous route by which loads travel from roof and floors through members to the ground.

concepts.title: Floor load
concepts.summary: A residential floor carries dead load (self-weight, finishes) and imposed load (people, furniture), combined with factors 1.35 and 1.5 for strength checks.

misconceptions: Learners think walls only hold up the roof; every opening needs a lintel to pass the load round it.
Learners think deeper beams are only about span; stiffness and vibration limit floors.
Learners mix kN/m^2 with kN/m.
sequence: Gravity loads and a path to the ground.
Walls and frames; lintels; foundations.
Area load to line load by joist spacing.
Moment M = wL^2/8.
Section modulus Z = b d^2/6 and allowable stress.
Joist deflection also limits the size (not computed here).
examples: Floor: dead 0.5, imposed 1.5 kN/m^2: design 1.35*0.5+1.5*1.5=2.925 kN/m^2. Joists at 0.4 m: 1.17 kN/m.
Span 3.6 m: M=1.17*3.6^2/8=1.895 kN m; with illustrative allowable 7 MPa, Z >= 271 cm^3.
A 47 x 195 mm joist has Z=47*195^2/6=297.9 cm^3, enough.

figures.learnerAction: Change the span and see the moment peak grow with the square.

lessons.title: Light
lessons.objective: Compute a daylight factor and test room depth against window height.

concepts.title: Daylight factor
concepts.summary: Indoor illuminance as a percentage of the unobstructed outdoor illuminance under an overcast sky.

concepts.title: Depth rule
concepts.summary: A side-lit room is adequately lit near the back if L/W + L/Hw is no more than 2/(1-R) for average surface reflectance R.

misconceptions: Learners judge a room by window area alone; position and height matter.
Learners treat a daylight factor as a measure of sun.
Learners think darker finishes have no effect.
sequence: Why light: seeing, mood, energy.
Daylight factor.
Windows: higher gives deeper light.
Depth rule.
Shading and glare: overhang and orientation.
Artificial light by inverse-square.
examples: 150 lux inside, 10 000 lux outside: DF=1.5 percent.
Room 5 m deep, 4 m wide, window head 2.2 m: 5/4+5/2.2=3.52, below 2/(1-0.5)=4, passes.
Window head 1.8 m: 1.25+2.78=4.03, fails.

lessons.title: Heat through a wall
lessons.objective: Compute a wall's U-value from its layers and the heat loss through it.

concepts.title: Thermal resistance
concepts.summary: R = thickness / conductivity (m^2 K/W) for a layer; resistances in series add.

concepts.title: U-value
concepts.summary: U = 1 / (Rsi + sum of R + Rse), in W/m^2 K; heat loss Q = U A dT.

misconceptions: Learners add U-values of layers. Add resistances, then invert.
Learners think thick means good; the conductivity is what matters.
Learners forget the surface resistances (0.13 inside, 0.04 outside).
sequence: Heat flows from warm to cold in proportion to the temperature difference.
A layer's resistance is thickness divided by conductivity.
Add the layer resistances and the two surface films, 0.13 inside and 0.04 outside.
Take the reciprocal to get the U-value.
Heat loss Q = U A dT.
Compare with regulatory targets and with a wall without insulation.
examples: 40 m^2 at 20 K difference: 138 W.
Removing insulation gives R=1.23, U=0.81, 4.7 times the loss.

figures.shows: Layer table with thickness, conductivity, R and a running total.
Temperature through the wall.

lessons.title: Air leakage, condensation and thermal bridges
lessons.objective: Compute ventilation heat loss and decide if a surface will condense.

concepts.title: Ventilation heat loss
concepts.summary: H = 0.33 n V in W/K for n air changes per hour and V in m^3.

concepts.title: Dew point
concepts.summary: The temperature at which air of a given moisture content becomes saturated, so water condenses on any colder surface.

misconceptions: Learners think more insulation fixes damp; poor ventilation or cold bridges cause condensation.
Learners think airtight buildings are unhealthy; they need controlled ventilation.
Learners ignore corners and lintels, which are cold.
sequence: Air carries heat out through gaps; count air changes per hour.
Ventilation heat loss = 0.33 x n x V.
Warm air holds more water vapour; cooled enough it reaches the dew point.
Compute the inside surface temperature and compare with dew point.
Thermal bridges such as lintels and corners are colder spots.
Design airtight and then ventilate deliberately.
examples: Wall U=0.173, 20 C inside, 0 C outside: inside surface 19.55 C. Old double glazing U=2.8: 12.72 C.
Dew point at 20 C: 12.0 at 60 percent RH, 13.2 at 65 percent, so the old window condenses at 65 percent.

lessons.title: Comfort and passive design
lessons.objective: Name the factors of thermal comfort, compute metabolic heat and apply passive strategies.

concepts.title: Comfort factors
concepts.summary: Air temperature, radiant temperature, air speed, humidity, clothing and activity together set comfort.

concepts.title: Passive design
concepts.summary: Using form, orientation, glazing, mass and ventilation to keep comfort with little energy.

misconceptions: Learners judge comfort by air temperature alone; cold walls feel cold at 21 C.
Learners think thermal mass warms a room; it stores and releases.
Learners think more glazing south always helps.
sequence: A person is a heat engine losing heat by radiation, convection and evaporation.
Comfort needs six things to line up: air and radiant temperature, air speed, humidity, clothing and activity.
Operative temperature averages air and radiant temperatures.
A person at 1 met gives off 58.2 W per square metre of skin, about 105 W.
Winter: gain sun, store it, retain it.
Summer: shade, ventilate at night, use mass.
examples: Air 20, walls 16: operative 18 C.
Seated office work at 1.2 met: 1.2*58.2*1.8=126 W.
A south window with a 0.6 m overhang at latitude 52 shades June sun and admits December sun.

figures.shows: A person with arrows for radiation, convection, evaporation.

lessons.title: Roofs, rain and damp
lessons.objective: Choose a roof form by pitch and compute rainwater flow and damp-course height.

concepts.title: Pitch
concepts.summary: The roof slope angle, rise over half the span.

concepts.title: Rainfall run-off
concepts.summary: Flow Q = i A, rainfall intensity times plan area.

misconceptions: Learners think a flat roof is flat; it falls to drains.
Learners use the sloped area for rain; use the plan area.
Learners think a damp-proof course is for rising damp only; it also stops splash.
sequence: A roof exists to move water away and keep weather out.
Roof forms: flat with falls, mono-pitch, gable, hip.
Pitch triangle: ridge rise = half-span x tan(pitch).
Rain flow = intensity x plan area.
Gutters and downpipes sized for the flow.
At the base of the wall, keep the damp course above the ground.
examples: Span 6 m, 30 degrees: ridge 3*tan30=1.73 m above the eaves.
Rise 1.0 m over half-span 2.5 m: pitch 21.8 degrees.

lessons.title: How a small building is drawn
lessons.objective: Name the drawings in a set, their usual scales, and what each is for.

concepts.title: Drawing set
concepts.summary: Site plan, floor plans, sections, elevations and details, each at a scale suited to what it must show.

concepts.title: Conventions
concepts.summary: Line weights, symbols, grid, dimensions and north arrow so the reader can build without asking.

misconceptions: Learners think one drawing shows everything.
Learners scale from a printed drawing on a different paper size.
Learners think drawings are art; they are instructions and a contract.
sequence: Who reads drawings: client, planner, builder.
Site plan 1:500 to 1:200.
Floor plans and sections 1:100 to 1:50.
Details 1:20 to 1:5.
Symbols: doors, windows, stairs, levels.
Project stages from brief to completion.
examples: A wall detail at 1:5: 100 mm is 20 mm on paper.
A 12 m wall at 1:100 is 120 mm.
A section cut thick, items beyond thin.

lessons.title: A small building, end to end
lessons.objective: Combine site, area, structure, light and heat to check a small cabin design.

concepts.title: Synthesis
concepts.summary: Each decision affects the others; check them against the brief.

concepts.title: Fabric first
concepts.summary: Reduce heat loss through the envelope before adding systems.

misconceptions: Learners treat topics separately.
Learners add features before checking the budget.
Learners forget the occupants.
sequence: Brief: a 6 m x 4 m cabin for two.
Orientation and glazing on the south face.
Gross area and cost.
Structure: joists, walls.
Heat loss: walls, floor, roof, glazing, ventilation.
Drawing set and what is left to decide.
examples: Footprint 6 x 4 = 24 m^2; at 85 percent efficiency, net 20.4 m^2.
Wall area 2*(6+4)*2.4 = 48 m^2 less 4 m^2 glazing = 44 m^2 at U 0.173 = 7.6 W/K; glazing 4 m^2 at 1.4 = 5.6 W/K.
Ventilation 24*2.4=57.6 m^3 at 0.5 ach: 9.5 W/K.
